transcript: Meeting header: 2026-03-25 14:00 UTC | Duration: 1h15m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Sharma - Redwood; Marta Ruiz, Devon Clark, Samir Patel, Tom Li - Atlas Payments

00:00 Alex: okay, uh, thanks everyone for joining. we wanted to run through a practical methodology for benchmarking across hosted, dedicated and private setups. this is a bit of a deep dive so we'll get into kv cache behavior and, uh, batching artifacts
00:22 Marta: great, thanks. our main ask is apples to apples. we see wildly different numbers depending on env and we need to be able to compare apples to apples before committing to dedicated nodes

00:35 Priya: totally, and that is exactly the crux. there are a bunch of factors that commonly get conflated: sequence length distribution in prompt sets, cache warmup state, batching configs, and also network variance for VPCs vs hosted. we'll try to break those down

00:52 Devon: quick context - our current stack runs a mix of short auth prompts (~40 tokens) and longer conversation continuations (~600 tokens), about 40% short, 60% long. throughput target is like 200 concurrent qps with p95 < 300ms for short ones

01:15 Alex: nice, that helps. when people say p95 < 300ms they often mean token latency vs end-to-end. important to nail definitions: are we measuring per-token generation latency, model infer wall-clock, or total request time including deserialization, network, and post-processing?
01:35 Samir: security side - we need to make sure any benchmark artifacts don't accidentally leak PII. prefer synthetic prompt sets derived from our templates

01:45 Priya: yeah, we usually recommend two prompt sets: (1) synthetic-but-realistic derived prompts for open benchmarks, (2) customer-provided representative set for final apples-to-apples. also capture sequence length histograms, since batching efficiency depends heavily on that

02:10 Alex: on the harness side we typically provide a load generator that supports variable seq length distribution, poisson inter-arrival, and the ability to pre-warm kv cache by re-playing prefixes. we'll share that repo after the call
02:28 Marta: how do you suggest measuring kv cache hit rate? our first numbers were noisy - sometimes cache hit seems high but latency doesn't improve

02:40 Priya: good question. there are two useful signals: internal runtime metrics (kv_cache_hits, kv_cache_misses, avg_kv_lookup_latency) and external buckets like measured p50/p95 for requests with cache-hit vs miss. you want to tag traces with kv_hit=true/false. note: some runtimes do approximate cache lookup stats which can be off
03:05 Devon: is kernel selection and quantization directly visible in the metrics? sometimes an int8 run performs worse due to kernel fallback

03:15 Priya: yes, kernel fallback and micro-kernel choices matter. on some GPU families int8 GEMM kernels exist for certain shapes; other shapes fall back to fp16 kernels and you lose the perf win. for apples-to-apples we recommend: same model architecture, same sequence bank, and compare fp16 vs quantized with identical batch distribution, and capture GPU kernel trace if possible
03:48 Tom: what's your advice for warm starts vs cold starts? our first POC had huge cold start variance during autoscale events

03:58 Alex: cold starts are painful. benchmark should separate steady-state latency from cold-start tails. run a baseline warmup phase until KV hit-rates and kernel JIT caches stabilize, then run the measurement window. record both: cold-start p99s during scale events, and steady-state p95s
04:20 Marta: okay. about VPC and on-prem: network latency to model servers in a peered VPC was adding 20-40ms in our tests. how should we simulate that in hosted tests?

04:32 Priya: we recommend introducing configurable network emulation (tc/netem) on the client or a proxy to reproduce RTT, packet loss, and jitter. treat that as an independent knob. also measure per-hop MTU fragmentation if you have large payloads (embeds or long prompts)
04:58 Devon: one thing that confused us: batching seems to improve throughput but sometimes increases p95 for short prompts. how to tune batching to meet strict latency SLOs?

05:10 Priya: yup this is classic. you want dynamic batching with latency budget. key knobs: max_batch_size, max_batch_latency_ms, and a weight distribution if you have mixed seq lengths. smaller max_batch_latency reduces tail but lowers throughput. also prefer prefix-based caching so short prompts hit cache and bypass some compute
05:38 Alex: we should document a recommended matrix of batch settings for different workload shapes. we'll include examples: short-tail dominated, long- seq dominated, and bimodal distributions
05:52 Samir: on compliance: for on-prem we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs of inference requests. how do we validate that during benchmarks?

06:05 Priya: for validation we typically run a compliance checklist: verify KMS-encrypted model keys, show inference logs are emitted to the customer's logging endpoint, strip PII from test prompts, and capture audit log entries for a sample run. share the SOC2 and network diagrams after - Alex will send those
06:25 Marta: good. back to apples-to-apples: what about model versions and tokenizer differences? small tokenizer tokenization variance can shift token counts and thus batching behavior

06:38 Priya: exactly. canonicalize tokenizer and token counts as part of pre-processing. fix the model repo/commit id for each run and record tokenizer vocab hash. always record tokens-per-request stats

06:52 Alex: wanted to flag measurement noise sources: GPU thermal throttling, other co-tenants on shared nodes, and even CUDA version mismatches. for dedicated runs we recommend an isolated node with pinned CUDA and driver versions and recorded environment snapshot
07:10 Devon: do you have recommended observability hooks to capture for root-cause? we currently only export p95 latency and GPU util

07:20 Priya: you want a combo: request-level traces (with kv_hit bool, batch_id, seq_length, tokens_generated), system metrics (GPU util, SM_efficiency, memory utilization, GPU temperature), kernel-level logs if available, and network metrics (RTT, retransmits). that allows correlating a p95 spike with CPU stalls or a large batch flush
07:50 Marta: can you walk us through an example benchmark run plan end-to-end?

08:00 Alex: sure - example 60-minute run plan: 1) provisioning + env snapshot (5m), 2) warmup phase with incremental qps to stabilize caches and kernel JITs (15m), 3) steady-state measurement window with target qps and controlled seq length distribution (30m), 4) scale/chaos events to capture cold start tails (5-10m), 5) teardown and artifact collection (5m). save raw traces and a summarized report with p50/p95/p99, throughput, kv_hit_rate, and GPU metrics
08:34 Tom: when you say warmup, how do you select prefixes for cache warmup? random or the actual most-common prefixes?

08:43 Priya: best practice: use a blend. seed warmup with heavy hitters from production (if allowed), then run a broader sweep of prefixes to increase cache coverage. measure kv hit-rate over time and stop warmup when hit-rate curve flattens
09:05 Devon: what about synthetic traffic - does it misrepresent real jitter? our real traffic is bursty around 09:00 UTC

09:14 Priya: synthetic is a necessary approximation. use Poisson or bursty arrival patterns and replay production inter-arrival histograms if you can export them. include a mix of cold and hot keys to mimic real cache pressure
09:30 Marta: how do we compare quantized int8 vs fp16 in an apples-to-apples way besides matching batch distribution? we noticed some quality drop on one of our prompt types

09:40 Priya: quality must be measured in an eval harness alongside perf. run the same prompt set and compare normalized likelihoods or task metrics (e.g., BLEU/EM for structured tasks or semantic similarity thresholds). if int8 shows quality regression, consider per-layer quantization or mixed-precision fallbacks. always include quality gates in the benchmark
10:05 Alex: also note that quantization can change tokenization in edge cases if post-processing differs. document the model artifact and quantization recipe used
10:18 Samir: in private/on-prem modes, what network aspects usually bite teams? NAT timeouts, MTU, and proxy timeouts

10:27 Priya: yep. and also TLS termination points. measure handshake times and cert validation cost. for large throughput, keep TLS session reuse or mTLS with session resumption enabled. record CPU usage on the reverse proxy - it often becomes the bottleneck
10:45 Devon: do you recommend running benchmarks within the customer's VPC (in the same subnet) versus peered? we worry about cross-az traffic costs and variance
10:55 Alex: run both if possible: colocated to measure pure model runtime, and peered to measure realistic network overhead. use netem to emulate the peered baseline if budget is constrained
11:10 Marta: curious - how do you instrument batch-level traces? we want to know which requests were coalesced into the same batch

11:20 Priya: include a batch_id label on trace spans. the load generator can tag requests so the runtime emits batch boundaries. then you can compute batch-size distributions and correlate batch-size to latency
11:40 Tom: any tips on measuring token-level latency vs request-level? our dashboard only shows request-level p95 currently

11:48 Priya: token-level requires instrumenting the runtime to emit per-token timestamps, but approximate approach: capture model output stream timestamps and infer per-token intervals. for true per-token, hook into the runtime's token emit hook. that helps identify whether p95 is due to slow token generation or slow first-token latency

12:10 Alex: quick callout about reproducibility: store random seeds, GPU clock settings, and driver versions in artifact metadata. use infra-as-code to recreate the exact instance types and driver stack
12:26 Marta: let's talk about the final report template - what should it include?

12:33 Alex: recommended sections: environment snapshot, prompt set details (token histograms), warmup curves (kv_hit_rate over time), measurement windows with p50/p95/p99, batch-size distribution, GPU/kernel traces, network emulation parameters, and quality eval results. include an appendix with raw traces and scripts to reproduce plots
12:55 Devon: you mentioned kernel traces earlier - is there an easy way to collect them? on some clouds we don't have access to nvprof

13:05 Priya: collect what you can: CUDA profiler on dedicated/on-prem, CUPTI traces if available, or if not possible, capture nvtx annotations from the runtime that mark kernel launches. even annotated timelines are helpful
13:20 Samir: for security review we'll need a short write-up of what telemetry is emitted during benchmarks and how long artifacts are retained
13:30 Alex: yes we'll include a telemetry matrix and retention policy in the artifact bundle. we'll also provide a sanitized artifact set for any public benchmark share
13:45 Marta: ok, sounds good. are there any gotchas when comparing hosted Redwood API numbers vs Dedicated?

13:54 Priya: hosted numbers often include network egress, front-door queuing, and multi-tenant variance. Dedicated gives you more isolation but you still need to control for kernel and batch configs. align on: same model commit, same tokenizer, same batch knobs, same warmup, and same prompt distribution
14:15 Devon: last question - how do you recommend we measure cost efficiency when comparing options? raw $/token is too coarse

14:25 Alex: agree. compute cost-per-successful-response at given SLO, e.g., $ per successful request under p95 target, and normalize by quality metrics (like passes QA threshold). include amortized infra costs, licensing, and networking costs. we'll share a cost-model spreadsheet
14:45 Marta: perfect. next steps?

14:50 Alex: recap: I'll share the harness, SOC2/network docs; Priya will run staging runs and attach kernel traces where possible; Devon will share VPC details and the prompt set; we'll reconvene after staging run completes
15:05 Marta: thanks everyone. we'll expect the repo and schedule the on-prem pilot after we see staging results
15:12 Alex: thanks, bye
15:20 [call ends]
